posts.title: Checked Against the Record
posts.excerpt: In a test case, a local coding agent says it updated two files and the records show one. What a harness can establish about its own turn, how it labels the claims it recognizes and cannot match, and what it states it did not check.
headings: What the harness changes, and what it does not
The approved payload is the written payload
posts.text:
In short. A model's answer is a claim about what happened. Talos, a local coding assistant, derives each turn's status from how it classified the request and from its own execution and verification records, labels file-change claims it recognizes and cannot match to those records, and prints what it did not assess. The model's weights are unchanged. The harness changes the conditions under which the model works and what the turn's report can be trusted to say.
Two files claimed, one edited
A test in the Talos codebase pins a simple case. The model's final answer says "I updated README.md and settings.json." The turn's execution records show one successful edit, to README.md. The test checks that the claim is flagged as unsupported. The label layout and the advisory status shown below follow from reading the code, and no test pins them.
Figure 1. The answer's claimed targets on one side, the turn's execution records on the other. README.md matches a recorded edit. settings.json has no record, so the answer is labeled. With no higher-priority outcome, the unsupported claim makes the status advisory.
Talos reads the answer for current claims of file changes by the assistant, resolves each named target against the workspace path, and compares it with the targets of recorded successful file operations. settings.json has no match, so the answer is prefixed with a label and a list of the unmatched targets.
The model's text follows unchanged below the label. Unless a stronger fact decides the status first, such as a partial change, the turn is classified as advisory instead of complete.
Until 16 October 2026 the same answer passed without a label. The old check was existential. Any successful edit anywhere in the turn suppressed it, so one real edit covered a claim about two files. The old label also ended with a sentence the runtime could not support, "No file on disk was actually modified." Talos records its own tool executions. It does not track an editor, a build script or another process writing to the same disk. The October change made the check per target and narrowed the label to what the records show. The published 0.10.8 beta still carries the old check and the old wording, so in that release the answer above passes without a label.
What the harness changes, and what it does not
A harness does not change the model's weights. It does change the conditions the model works under, and with them what the complete system accomplishes in some cases. A file-change request that produces no tool call gets one bounded retry with a nudge toward the write tools. A workspace question answered without reading anything is retried with read tools, and the runtime can read a file and hand its content to the model.
Those interventions can also go wrong. In a recorded run on 18 October 2026, on a development build from that day, the retry that followed a model's first reply dropped the conversation history, the file content and the textual tool schemas, and the model's second attempt produced an invalid edit. The code that builds that retry request is unchanged at the commit described here. The same compaction drops a note the runtime prepares when a model denies it can access files, so that note never reaches the model.
So the subject of this piece is narrower than model quality. It is what the runtime can establish about a turn, and how it reports what it cannot.
Status comes from records
A completed Talos turn ends with one of eight classifications. They are verified, unverified, read-only answered, partial, blocked by approval, blocked by policy, advisory and failed. No success classification is taken from the model's prose. The prose can only lower a status, through the claim check above and a few other lexical checks, such as withheld command output or a recognized denial of file access.
A request that requires a file change, where the model never calls a file tool, ends as blocked by policy. A test named for the rule, requiredMutationWithoutToolsStaysIncompleteRegardlessOfNarrative, feeds seven narratives, among them quoted, passive and proposed ones, and checks that none lets such a turn count as complete.
Verified is reached only when a verifier passed or a required verification command succeeded. For an exact edit it means the approved replacement was observed in the file after the edit under the verifier's checks. It does not mean the fix is correct.
A change no verifier could check is reported as complete but unverified, with a neutral marker instead of the success glyph, and a line that begins "[File write/readback passed. No task-specific verifier was applicable, so task completion was not verified."
When static verification fails on a turn whose changes all applied, the turn becomes failed and the model's success summary is replaced by the runtime's result, with the sentence "The assistant success summary was replaced with this runtime verification result because verification failed."
When several facts apply, a fixed order decides, and it shows which facts outrank a false claim.
Malformed tool-call text in an answer that called no tool, or invalid change arguments when no change succeeded, make the turn failed.
A denied command blocks it by approval, and a failed command fails it.
A change refused by a read-only mode, or a required change with no tool call, blocks it by policy.
A denied change or a denied protected read blocks it by approval. A protected read that never got approval blocks it by policy.
A partial change makes it partial.
Failed verification makes it failed.
On a request that asks only for verification, a successful required command makes it verified.
Advisory facts, among them an unsupported change claim, missing evidence or an ungrounded answer, make it advisory.
A passing verifier makes it verified.
A request that asked for no change is read-only answered, and anything else is complete but unverified.
Rule 7 comes before rule 8, so a request that asked only for verification ends as verified when its required command succeeded, even if the model also claimed an edit it did not make. The runtime then replaces the answer with a one-line summary of the command's result, so neither the claim nor the label is shown, and the turn's trace keeps only a fixed warning that an unsupported change claim was made, without its text or targets.
Unless a failed change left effects on disk, the post-apply verifier runs only when the facts known before it leave the turn complete or partial. A turn already advisory because of an unsupported claim is not checked by it, so an edit that applied but broke the file can leave that turn advisory instead of failed.
After an interactive turn that does not end in an error, the terminal also prints the work outcome and the line Whole-request coverage: not assessed, unless the timing display is turned off in the settings. The runtime checks parts of a request, such as named targets, but never whether the whole request was satisfied, and the output says so.
What the claim check recognizes
The detection is not a model judging a model. It is a bounded lexical grammar over 27 verb forms, described in its own source as "Bounded lexical attribution of answer claims. No execution evidence is inferred from prose." That makes it predictable and testable. It also sets its limits.
Negations, proposals, reported or rejected quotations, changes attributed to someone else and abstract objects are left alone. "I updated my assessment" is not a file claim. A bare quotation of a change claim gets the weaker label.
A first-person claim whose time cannot be resolved, or a claim placed in this turn without a clear actor, gets a weaker label, which says the records do not establish it, instead of calling it false. A passive claim with no actor and no time, such as "the README has been updated", gets no label.
Some verbs are outside the grammar. "Fixed", "added" and "implemented" are among them, so "I fixed the bug in calc.py" passes unlabeled.
A claim that names no file passes when any file change in the turn succeeded, unless it says all, every or each, which gets the weaker label.
The check does not run when a change in the turn was denied, when a failed change left applied or uncertain effects, or when the only changes were invalid calls. Those turns get their own deterministic summaries.
Target names are compared exactly, including letter case. On a case-insensitive file system that can label a true claim about Readme.md as unsupported, which is the safer error.
Some runtime messages still use the broad wording the October change removed from the label, for example [Action obligation failed: no file was changed in this turn.]. That message is accurate only for Talos's own tools.
The approved payload is the written payload
Approval only means something if the approved change is the change that lands. Before anything is shown to the user, Talos may transform a proposed write in several ways. Among them are removal of markdown commentary the model wrapped around the content, an exact-literal correction that restores a payload the user dictated word for word, path canonicalization, and preservation of the file's existing line endings, byte order mark and final newline.
All of these run before the approval preview is built. The preview, the approval prompt, the checkpoint and the write are then built from the same call content, and nothing changes it between approval and execution. The commentary sanitizer is documented as non-idempotent, so a second pass could strip legitimate content. It has one production caller, and the write tools are documented not to sanitize again.
After the write, the tool reads the file back and compares the text with what it wrote. A mismatch fails the call as an integrity failure, after the file was already replaced, so the checkpoint is the undo path. A test named writeContentSanitizedBeforeApprovalSoApprovedBytesAreWrittenBytes checks that the file on disk equals the sanitized payload, that the approval showed the byte count that landed, and that the trace hash matches the approval hash.
The precise guarantee is about what is built and written. The person approving sees a preview and a diff that may be shortened, not every byte.
What is not checked
Some of these limits are written into the project's documentation, and a test fails the build if that wording drifts. Others come from reading the code and from one recorded run.
Read-only explanations may remain unverified. A wrong explanation of code that changed nothing is not caught.
Claims about command output are withheld only for recognized shapes, such as a git status, a test run or a file listing, when no matching tool result exists.
A no-tool turn that was not a change request is not checked for change claims.
Claim detection is lexical, so paraphrases outside the grammar pass.
Traces and logs are not tamper-evident. There is no hash chain, signature or append-only enforcement.
In the 18 October run the harness itself produced misleading text. A correct answer was replaced by "did not complete" text, which the code now prevents but no live run has rechecked. A question about a bug got a "[Path existence verified]" banner, and that trigger is still present.
The README draws the boundary in two sentences. "Talos is a governance shell around local model execution, not proof that the model is capable or honest without runtime evidence. A documented limitation is not an overclaim."
What transfers
Derive a turn's status from execution and verification records, and let the model's prose only lower it.
Match change claims per target. One real edit must not cover a claim about two files.
Scope every runtime message to what the runtime can observe. A tool log cannot speak for the whole disk.
Build the preview, the approval and the write from the same payload, after every transform.
Print what was not assessed, every time, instead of leaving it implied.
The model's prose is kept, kept under a label, or replaced by runtime text, and pass markers the model wrote for itself are removed. What can be held to account is the turn's report about the model.
Described as of the local development commit de779a78, 27 October 2026, which has not been pushed. The published 0.10.8 developer beta predates the claim attribution grammar and its per-target check, the whole-request status line, write-format preservation and the fix that keeps an admitted answer when a read-only completeness retry is exhausted, all described here. That fix exists only in this commit.

posts.title: Inside a Trust Harness, in Java 21
posts.excerpt: One edit request followed through a local coding assistant written in plain Java 21. Where a model's suggestion becomes an action, which part of the runtime owns each step, and where the containment stops.
headings: Where to look in the code
posts.text:
In short. Talos is a command-line assistant for developer workspaces that runs a local model through llama.cpp. The model only proposes. A deterministic runtime decides what a turn may do, a person approves changes where the policy asks, and a record says what happened. The runtime governs what Talos launches and writes. It is not an operating-system sandbox, and the boundary is drawn below.
The architecture overview states one rule, that "model output is never enough evidence by itself." The runtime's policy, approval, verification and trace code is organized around that sentence. The codebase is plain Java 21 with no application framework, 890 main source files and 193,597 lines, with a test source set of 935 files and a separate end-to-end test source set.
Figure 1. One turn, two authorities and the host boundary. The model lane proposes. The runtime lane decides, executes and records. File operations stay in the workspace, while an approved build runs with the user's own permissions.
One request, end to end
Take a request such as "In settings.py, change TIMEOUT from 30 to 60."
A contract before the model. The runtime first resolves the request into a task contract, here a file edit with a change requested and allowed and settings.py as the expected target. The resolver is deterministic code. The contract's own documentation says it is "not a planner and not an LLM classifier."
A ceiling from the mode. The session's mode applies a posture to that contract. In a read-only mode the contract is rewritten so that no change is allowed, whatever the request said.
A tool surface. From the contract, the runtime picks the tools this turn may use, here the read tools plus the edit and write tools. The system prompt describes only those tools, and the model call is filtered to the same list.
The proposal. The model answers with a tool call, typically native tool_calls from llama.cpp, or a tool call written as text when native calling is unavailable. Either way it is a proposal.
The checks. The proposed call passes a fixed sequence of an unknown-tool check, the current-turn surface check, normalization of the payload, phase policy and validation. Then the permission policy decides allow, ask or deny.
The approval. For a file edit the default is ask. The terminal shows the call with a unified diff preview, capped at 60 lines and 6,000 characters, and waits. End of input or Ctrl-C denies.
A checkpoint. With checkpointing on, the default, a content-addressed checkpoint of the target is taken after approval and before the write. A failed checkpoint blocks the change.
The write and the check. The edit runs inside the workspace boundary, the file is read back, and a verifier checks that the approved replacement is present. The turn ends with a completion status, guards compare the model's final answer with the records, and a JSON trace of the turn is written.
Three of those steps carry most of the design. They are the contract, the tool surface and the way commands run.
The contract is code
Posture is applied to the contract as a record and an early return.
The turn plan built from that contract is also a record. Its compact constructor recompiles the task expectations from the contract and throws if a caller passed different ones, so the plan's expectations, request obligation and requested results cannot disagree with the contract. Its tool lists are not checked there. They are enforced at the point of use.
One surface, enforced twice
The tools the model is told about and the tools the runtime accepts come from the same plan. The prompt is the weaker enforcement, because prompt text is advice to a model. The second enforcement runs in the turn processor before approval and before any file is touched.
When no surface has been set, this check passes. Every mode that calls the model sets one during turn preparation. Two tests pin the property for native calls and for calls written as JSON text, each outside the dispatched surface and each rejected before approval or IO. A retry cannot widen the surface. The dispatcher throws when an escalated retry would exceed "the captured current-turn authority".
Files the user pins into context are framed in the prompt as "untrusted workspace file content" and "reference data only". That framing is prompt wording, and the documentation's general rule applies to it. Prompt wording is not security. The enforcement is the surface check and the permission policy.
Commands, and where containment stops
Talos has a command tool and no general shell tool. talos.run_command takes a profile id. Raw command shapes are refused by key before planning.
A matching parameter ends with "Raw shell commands are not supported. Use an approved command profile." The built-in profiles that talos.run_command accepts are five Gradle tasks, each run with --no-daemon. Arguments are checked per profile in a switch expression, and the five Gradle profiles share one grammar. Gradle profiles accept only --tests <selector>, --stacktrace and --info, and caller arguments are screened against fixed lists of shell operators, network tokens and destructive tokens. The command reaches ProcessBuilder as an argument list, with standard input closed and the process tree killed on timeout.
A workspace can declare its own profiles in .talos/profiles.yaml. They register only when the file's raw bytes match a SHA-256 pin stored outside the workspace, in the Talos home directory. A byte change returns them to untrusted, a corrupt pin fails closed, and trust is checked again at planning and before execution. The declaration file is also a protected path. A model that edits the workspace cannot add a profile by editing it.
Profiles narrow what Talos launches and with which arguments. They do not contain what the launched program does.
A Gradle task runs the workspace's own wrapper and build scripts, which are executable code and run with the user's permissions.
Build scripts are ordinary workspace files. A model can propose edits to them. Such a write can ride a remembered write approval or a configured allow rule, and only the command run is always asked again, unless an allow rule covers it too.
The plan description Talos prints for each command says it directly, "host network is not isolated".
A trusted workspace profile may name any executable, and the Gradle wrapper itself is a shell script on POSIX and a batch file run by cmd.exe on Windows.
There is no container, restricted token or network namespace. The approval prompt is the boundary before a command runs, and the operating system's normal permissions are the boundary after.
Permission as an ordered ladder
The permission policy is read top to bottom. A path that escapes the workspace is denied. A change to a protected path is denied without a prompt. Then come configured deny rules, protected reads that require asking, configured ask rules and configured allow rules. Read-only tools default to allow. Everything else asks.
Remembered approval is narrow. A session can remember approval for file writes inside the workspace, apart from writes under .github, while destructive calls, typed workspace operations and command execution always ask again. A command never rides on an approval given to a file write. A configured allow rule, however, does skip the prompt, which is the point of configuring one, unless a scope warning or a change to the file's line endings, byte order mark or final newline forces an ask.
What Java 21 contributes
Records carry the turn's data. The main source tree has 815 record declarations. The task contract has 11 components, the turn plan 19 and the trace record 20, and compact constructors are where some of their invariants are checked.
Four sealed hierarchies exist. The most used is Result, the output of a turn. Switches over it are exhaustive with no default branch, so a new result kind is a compile error at every switch that forgot it. In this excerpt the comments are trimmed.
Unnamed patterns are a preview feature in Java 21, so each unused binding carries a name.
Concurrency is plain. A turn runs synchronously. Virtual threads appear in four auxiliary places, such as indexing. A child process's output is drained by daemon platform threads in a fixed pool, and a comment in the runner explains that pipe reads and close() can ignore interruption, so cleanup runs on those workers and never on the caller. Record patterns, structured concurrency and scoped values are not used.
The main dependencies are Lucene 10.2.2 for retrieval, JLine 3.30.13 and picocli 4.7.6 for the terminal, Jackson 2.17.1 for JSON and YAML, PDFBox and POI for document text, HtmlUnit for static web checks, sqlite-jdbc, SLF4J with Logback, java-diff-utils for approval diffs and ArchUnit 1.4.2 for architecture tests, built with Gradle 8.14. The release build produces a per-user Windows MSI through jpackage, an app zip, a Linux app-image archive, a CycloneDX SBOM and checksums files.
Boundaries the build enforces
Package direction is checked twice in gradle check. A source scan applies six dependency rules against a baseline file of accepted violations that is currently empty. An ArchUnit test applies eleven rules to the compiled bytecode. One of them keeps the tool-call loop from depending on the terminal layer. Its reason clause is trimmed here.
The runtime does not depend on the terminal packages. The terminal layer implements interfaces the runtime owns instead, among them RuntimeTurnContext, TurnRouter and ApprovalGate.
The package map presents its diagram as a target shape, and the code has not fully reached it. The turn executor, the model dispatcher and the outcome classifier still live in the terminal modes package, and the turn executor alone is 3,444 lines. A guard against new violations is not a claim that the old structure is finished.
The model at arm's length
Talos runs one model backend, llama.cpp. By default it launches and owns the server, which binds only to 127.0.0.1. Before launch it refuses a port that already has a listener, with "Another server is not restarted by Talos." After launch it checks that the listener belongs to the process it started, by process id and start time, and an observation it cannot make fails closed. The probe's documentation disclaims a hostile kernel and a race between the last check and the request. A connect_only mode attaches to an existing server instead of launching one.
For GPT-OSS, the Harmony chat format is applied by llama.cpp's embedded template. Talos does not parse Harmony tokens.
The trace
With session persistence on, the default, each turn writes a local JSON trace, schema version 5. It holds the contract, the tool surfaces, permission decisions, approvals, checkpoints, executions, verification and the rendered outcome. In the trace, prompts, answers and file contents are reduced to hashes and counts, while file paths, tool names and the parts of the request that name a target are kept. The turn log written beside it stores the request and the committed answer as plain text.
The trace is evidence for review, not an integrity guarantee. The documentation states that traces and logs are not tamper-evident. There is no hash chain, no signature and no append-only enforcement. A documentation test fails the build if the maintained docs drop that statement or use the word "tamper-proof".
Where to look in the code
Step Owner
Contract TaskContractResolver, TaskContract
Posture CapabilityPosturePolicy
Tool surface ToolSurfacePlanner, CurrentTurnPlan
Model call TurnModelDispatcher
Tool loop ToolCallLoop, capped at 10 iterations
Checks and execution TurnProcessor
Permission DeclarativePermissionPolicy
Commands CommandToolPlanner, CommandArgumentPolicy, ProcessCommandRunner
Verification StaticTaskVerifier
Trace LocalTurnTrace
What transfers
Resolve what a turn may do before asking the model anything, in code a test can pin.
Derive the prompt's tool list and the runtime's accepted list from one plan, and enforce the runtime list where it matters, before approval and before IO.
Replace a shell with named profiles and arguments checked per profile, and say plainly that a profile is not a sandbox.
Let records and sealed types carry decisions, so a missing case is a compile error.
Check package direction in the build, against an empty baseline.
Described as of the local development commit de779a78, 27 October 2026, which has not been pushed. The published 0.10.8 developer beta predates several of the changes described here, including the removal of the Ollama backend.

posts.title: Twelve Local Models, One Harness That Checks Them
posts.excerpt: Twelve open-weight models went through a qualification protocol in July 2026. Six finished a 72-trial run and passed every trust gate in every trial. Forty-three of the 102 failed trials were results affected by runtime or scoring behavior, so those results cannot be treated as clean measurements of model quality.
headings: Most early stops were about the request format
When the harness is part of the result
posts.text:
In short. Twelve open-weight models, from 3B to 24B parameters, went through the qualification protocol of Talos, a local coding assistant, on one desktop in July 2026. The six that completed a 72-trial run passed every trust gate in every trial, a joint result of the model and the runtime checks around it, and did the work unevenly. Forty-three of the 102 failed trials were results affected by runtime or scoring behavior. Those results cannot be treated as clean measurements of model quality, so the protocol measured Talos alongside the models. These are descriptive results from one machine and one engine build, not a ranking.
Talos runs a local model through llama.cpp, and every tool call the model makes is a proposal the runtime checks before it takes effect. Knowing whether a model calls tools when it should, abstains when it should and finishes the work it starts takes a protocol. The results below come from the packets it left behind, scorecards, per-trial results, final files and traces, and from the reports written beside them.
Figure 1. Twelve candidates, where each one stopped, and the population the results below describe.
The protocol
Each candidate passes through fixed stages. A failed stage stops that configuration, and a material change, such as a new request layout, starts a new configuration identity.
Acquisition. The exact source revision, bytes, size, SHA-256 and license are frozen. Where an official repository did not publish the needed quantization, a local conversion was made twice, and both outputs were byte-identical.
Engine preflight. The pinned llama.cpp server answers short direct probes, a request with no tools and one that must call a tool, with server-default sampling and output caps of 64 and 256 tokens. Some candidates were probed with a single user message, others with two short system messages before it. These probes are simpler than the requests Talos really sends.
Installed preflight. talos doctor --start runs eight probes on the installed build and projects the time of a reference turn.
Admission. Twelve scenarios, one fresh trial each, captured from a real terminal.
Full qualification. 24 scenarios across eight archetypes, from simple tasks to privacy, recovery and context pressure, three repetitions each, 72 fresh trials.
Every trial is checked against eight trust gates, among them approval integrity, mutation scope, completion truth and read-evidence binding. A failed trust gate blocks the candidate before any task score is read. The runbook keeps Talos's own faults apart. "A Talos defect is not a model failure. Record it separately, add a failing regression test, fix it, and start a fresh campaign identity."
The scorecard maps to two tiers. Accepted beta needs at least 20 of 24 scenarios, every archetype at 2 of 3, required-tool accuracy of 0.90, abstention of 0.95, requirement coverage of 0.85 and no timeouts. Experimental selectable needs 16 of 24 scenarios, required-tool accuracy of 0.75 and abstention of 0.90, with looser limits. The scorecard is an input to a human decision, and the product status of a model is set in one place, the model catalog in code. The lifecycle document puts it plainly. "Passing admission is not a support claim."
Where the twelve stopped
Model Furthest stage Scorecard result Catalog status at the pin
Ministral 3 3B admission, first trial stopped, template rejected the request not listed
Ministral 3 8B engine preflight stopped, template rejected the request not listed
Ministral 3 14B engine preflight stopped, template rejected the request not listed
Qwen2.5 Coder 7B engine preflight stopped, no native tool call not listed
Devstral Small 2507 (24B) engine preflight stopped, no native tool call not listed
Qwen2.5 Coder 14B admission (protocol v2) passed 12 of 12, no 72-trial run accepted beta, on an earlier record
GPT-OSS 20B full (protocol v4), tuned placement experimental selectable accepted beta, on an earlier record
Qwen3 8B full (protocol v5) experimental selectable experimental
Granite 4.1 3B full (protocol v5) experimental selectable experimental
Qwen3 4B full (protocol v5) experimental selectable experimental
Granite 4.1 8B full (protocol v5) experimental selectable experimental
Qwen3.5 9B full (protocol v5), after a request-layout adapter experimental selectable experimental
All six complete runs scored in the experimental tier. The two models the catalog lists as accepted beta hold that status through an evidence record dated 3 July 2026, made before this protocol.
Most early stops were about the request format
Counting Qwen3.5 9B's first configuration with the five candidates above, four of the six early stops ended on a request the chat template rejected before any token was generated. For the three Ministral models the server returned Jinja Exception: Only user, assistant and tool roles are supported, got system. Talos normally sends its instructions as two system messages, and their templates rejected that shape. For Qwen3.5 9B it returned "System message must be at the beginning." For Qwen3.5 an explicit layout was added that merges only Talos's own system frames into one leading message, and with it Qwen3.5 passed admission 12 of 12. The Ministral models were not retried under the adapter, so their result describes their templates and Talos's request shape, not what the models can do with tools.
The other two models answered, but not with a native tool call. In a one-message probe with server-default sampling and a 256-token cap, Qwen2.5 Coder 7B described a JSON call in prose, added an XML example and hit the cap. The probe did not use the near-greedy settings Talos applies to tool turns, so the rejection covers that configuration only. Its preflight report draws the lesson. "/props proves that the template can represent tools. It does not prove that the model reliably uses the representation." Devstral's template did not advertise tool support at all, and the model wrote read_local_file_tool(input: {"file_path": "README.md"}) as plain text.
What did not fail
These results cover the 432 trials of the six complete runs.
No trust gate failed.
No trial timed out, and no final answer reached the output limit. In two Qwen3 4B trials the first 512-token cap cut a tool turn short, and the uncapped retry then looped.
745 of 745 native tool calls were schema-valid, and no malformed call went unrecovered in 917 tool-eligible generations.
Every abstention was correct, 90 of 90.
306 of 324 required-tool decisions were correct.
For the six models that went on to a full run, the shape of a tool call stopped being the problem. That is a statement about Talos plus the model, not the model alone. Earlier, stopped attempts are not part of these numbers. In those packets 19 trials failed a trust gate, each recorded at the time as a Talos runtime defect, and at least two were later traced to the validator rather than the runtime.
What did fail
Figure 2. 24 scenarios by six models, successful repetitions out of three, with the cells where the harness or the scorer shaped the result marked.
Some failures were in the work.
Narrow searches. Asked to locate a service port, Granite 4.1 3B in all three trials and Qwen3 4B in one never read config.json. Where a model answered "not found" without reading the right file, Talos replaced the unsupported negative with a bounded disclosure, and the trial was scored as a model failure with every trust gate intact.
Exact output. Asked to "return only the current status value", Qwen3 8B wrapped the value draft in a full sentence in all three repetitions. The fact was right and the format was not.
Repetition loops. Qwen3 4B looped on the simplest read scenario in all three repetitions, and the repetition guard aborted each one with an empty answer.
Unsupported detail. Asked for a cross-document summary, Granite 4.1 3B searched one or two of the three documents with grep, read none of them, and added architectural detail they did not contain. No mechanical check scores added detail, so the scenario failed it for leaving out two required facts and for searching where a file read was required. The read-evidence gate stayed true, because that gate "proves which files were read, not whether every natural-language sentence is entailed by those files."
The six also differed in ways one score hides. Qwen3 4B covered the most scenarios, 20 of 24, and chose the required tool least often, 47 of 54. Granite 4.1 3B was the fastest and lightest, with a median turn of 2.41 seconds and a working set of about 3.2 GiB.
When the harness is part of the result
A reading of the raw packets on 27 October 2026 found four scenarios whose results are not clean model measurements, two for all six models and two for one or two models each. Those results hold 43 of the 102 failed trials. That does not make all 43 harness failures, since some include model-side misses as well. It means those trials cannot be read as measurements of the model alone. The historical scorecards are unchanged, and no corrected model score follows from these observations.
The two-part edit, all six models. The scenario asks for a page's heading to become "Atlas Control" and its status paragraph to start with "Offline". Every trial had exactly two model generations, a read and an edit. Both parts were in one file, and Talos ends the tool loop once every expected target has been changed, so after the first successful edit no model was asked for anything more. Five models had sent only the heading edit. Qwen3.5 9B sent both edits in one response, and the scenario's approve-once policy denied the second. Whether the other five would have completed the second part was never observed.
The static-page explanation, all six models. 15 of the 18 final answers are byte-identical to a template Talos itself renders. The other three are a Talos evidence notice, issued because Granite 4.1 3B did not read the script file. The scenario requires the word "Ready", which the template never contains. Granite's three trials therefore mix a model-side miss with a runtime-rendered answer.
A two-item privacy answer, Qwen3.5 9B and GPT-OSS 20B. Qwen3.5 numbered its items with two spaces after the number, and the scorer's pattern accepts exactly one. GPT-OSS 20B's one miss on the row is a two-rule answer whose indented sub-bullets the same pattern counted as six items. Qwen3.5's only miss against the accepted-beta thresholds was the scenario count, 19 of 24. Counted, this row would have raised it to 20 of 24 with every other threshold met, and the tier would still be a reviewed decision.
A yes-or-no question, Granite 4.1 3B. The prompt asks for a yes or no answer, and the scorer compares case-sensitively with No. Granite answered no three times and scored 0 of 3. Nothing in the prompt asked for a capital letter. The evaluator required capitalization that the prompt did not specify, so these three failures do not establish an incorrect yes-or-no answer.
The harness was also tested first. For Qwen2.5 Coder 14B and Qwen3 8B, the halted campaigns stopped because of Talos or its evidence capture, not the model, among them a prompt that asked for an answer "without opening any workspace file" and still produced read calls and a Ctrl-C turned into a second model request. Five of the nine incomplete Granite 4.1 3B full runs also ended on a trial recorded as a Talos runtime defect. Each Talos defect was fixed on the development branch and the campaign restarted under a new identity. The fixes are not yet released, and whether released 0.10.8 has the same defects was not tested, since every campaign ran a later development commit.
Setup
Every packet ran on one desktop, with an NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti with 16 GB of VRAM, an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X, 128 GB of RAM, Windows 11 and llama.cpp b9918 on CUDA 13.3, with one quantization per model. The usual context was 8,192 tokens. GPT-OSS 20B and the Qwen2.5 Coder 14B admission ran at 16,384, and GPT-OSS 20B's full run placed part of its expert weights on the CPU under a 5,120 MiB allocation limit, which its calibration guide calls "capacity simulation on a 16 GiB host." An older measurement on the same machine shows what the GPU does. A Qwen2.5 Coder 14B code-writing turn took 29.4 seconds on CUDA and hit the 300-second budget on the CPU build.
Turns that must call a tool run near-greedy, with temperature 0.2, top_p 0.8 and top_k 20, after earlier byte-identical requests produced both valid calls and protocol debris under default sampling. They start with an output cap of 512 tokens for reads and 1,024 for changes, and a call cut short is retried once without the cap. The Qwen3 models run with reasoning off. All runs used one backend. Released 0.10.8 already defaults to llama.cpp, and on 18 October 2026 the development branch removed Ollama entirely.
No profile carries a Low, Medium or High hardware label. The five profiles qualified in July each disclaim a weak-hardware, low-resource or minimum-hardware claim, and the two accepted profiles state RAM minimums no physical hardware packet has measured.
What the evidence supports
On this machine, with this build and these protocols, open-weight models from 3B to 20B passed every trust gate together with Talos and did the work unevenly. Two searched too narrowly, four padded exact answers and one added detail no file supported. GPT-OSS 20B reached the tool-call limit in ten read trials, and outside the two-part edit, twelve change requests across three models ended partial or failed. A large share of the failed trials sat in scenarios shaped by Talos itself, a stop rule, a rendered template and two answer keys, and those trials cannot be read as measurements of the models alone.
Each scenario ran three times, so the confidence intervals are broad.
The campaigns ran on different Talos commits, GPT-OSS under protocol v4 and the others under v5. Their own reports call the cross-model tables descriptive, not a controlled benchmark.
The protocol in code at the pin is v6, and no model has run it. Qualification has been frozen since 16 July while Talos kept changing.
The two accepted profiles rest on the 3 July record. Qwen2.5 Coder 14B has no 72-trial run, and GPT-OSS 20B's request layout has changed since that record.
What transfers
Probe with the exact request the agent sends, including its system messages and sampling. A template that passed a one-message probe rejected the real request on its first trial.
Run turns that must call a tool near-greedy with an output cap, and check what the uncapped retry does. Here it fired twice, both for Qwen3 4B, and both retries looped until the repetition guard stopped them.
Do not let the loop close a multi-part task on the first successful write. Here Talos ended every two-part edit after the first change, and the scorer counted the missing part against the model.
Separate harness effects from model behavior before scoring. Here 43 of the 102 failed trials were results the runtime or the scorer shaped.
Score only what the prompt asked for. A key that requires an unstated capital letter measures the key.
Evidence. Unpublished local qualification packets and reports dated 10 to 15 July 2026 and a performance review dated 8 July 2026, read on 27 October 2026. Talos code and documentation as of the local development commit de779a78, 27 October 2026, which has not been pushed.

posts.title: My 1st Year as a Software Engineer, Lessons Learned
posts.excerpt: Reflections on my first year as a software engineer, embracing challenges, asking for help, and the importance of kindness.
headings: 3. Don't be afraid to ask for more help
4. Understand the problem before writing code
5. Be kind and patient with yourself and others
posts.text:
As I look back on my first year in this job, I realize that I learned more than I ever thought possible. Even if there are many challenges along the way, I wouldn't trade the experience for anything. Here are some of the most important things I've learned so far.
1. Embrace creativity and challenge
One of the things that made me follow this career path was the opportunity to be creative and solve complex problems. I quickly learned that this can also be one of the most challenging aspects of this job. However, there were many times that I struggled to come up with a solution to a complex problem or times that I felt like I was at a dead end.
Even so, I also found that these moments of struggle often led to breakthroughs and new insights. So, the first lesson that I've learned is to embrace the creative and challenging aspects of the job and don't be afraid to push yourself outside of your comfort zone.
2. Turning Roadblocks into Learning Opportunities
As a new software engineer, I often felt like I needed to prove myself and show that I was capable of solving any problem at any time. Guess what, NO! I've miserably failed!
I quickly realized that there were many cases when my best efforts were not enough to solve a problem or complete a task and this can be discouraging. Despite this, it's important to acknowledge these moments as opportunities for growth and learning. Instead of giving up or becoming frustrated, I focused on what I could do to improve and move forward.
And this is the second lesson I learned the hard way. Recognize that your best efforts may not always be enough, but also remember that these moments of struggle can lead to valuable insights and growth.
3. Don't be afraid to ask for more help
This is important. If I could turn back the time in my first six months of work I would tell myself this.
"You are here to learn! So, ask more! They want it and you can't handle everything by yourself!"
Often, I struggled with a problem for hours, only to find out that a colleague had already solved a similar issue and could offer me advice. Asking for help is not a sign of weakness, but rather a strength and a willingness to learn.
Also, don't worry, eventually, all this knowledge you will gain by asking will be returned to the team in code implementation soon! So, my advice to new developers (like me) is to not be afraid to ask for help when you need it and engage with your colleagues. Your colleagues and seniors are there to support you and help you grow.
4. Understand the problem before writing code
Take a moment and think of the title above. It's easy to get caught up in the details of the code and the tools you're using, so it's important to remember that software engineering is ultimately about solving business problems. It is essential to provide the best solution.
By taking the time to understand the business logic and the problem, I was able to come up with more effective and efficient solutions. Take the time to understand the problem before diving into writing code.
5. Be kind and patient with yourself and others
Last but not least, the most important lesson I learned is to be kind and respectful to everyone. Don't fuel your mind with thoughts like "lesser than", or "better than" as comparison and competition only serve to create unnecessary stress and tension.
Focus on being consistent with your work whenever possible and be patient with yourself as you move forward. Experience will come with time and effort but kindness and patience are qualities that will serve you through your career.
These experiences have helped me to become a better developer and a more collaborative team member. Thank you for reading my thoughts and I hope that you'll find this helpful if you are at the beginning of your career!

posts.title: The Work-Test Cycle
posts.excerpt: How Talos is built. An edit loop and a release gate, six gates in one task, one record per batch, and a few distinctions kept apart. A focused pass is not acceptance, an exit code is not a result, and review agreement is not execution evidence.
headings: What is automated, and what is not
posts.text:
In short. Talos, a local coding assistant written in Java, is built with two loops. An edit loop runs while code changes and ends with the required local gates, and a release gate runs only for a candidate. The procedure asks for one short record per coherent batch, and the October records hold the exact commands, source hashes and results of each run. The examples below come from the author's unpublished October 2026 records, and the procedure they follow is about a month old in its current form.
A green suite, and 132 failures
In October 2026 a Windows CI run of Talos failed 132 of 13,254 unit tests. The end-to-end, coverage and final check steps never ran. The local suite was green, and none of the 132 was a product defect.
The GitHub runner's temporary folder is an 8.3 short-name alias, C:\Users\RUNNER~1\..., and the checkout sits on drive D:. 113 tests had bound a workspace at the unresolved temporary path while the product resolves real paths. 16 used fake model-artifact identities that returned the configured path where the product records the real one. One test expected a configured model path where the model library stores the real one. One relativized a C: path against a D: working directory. One timing test exceeded a three-second wall-clock limit on the runner.
The repair took a day and weakened no product check. Its one production change was a package-private counter in one class, read only by a test. A local lane was built to reproduce the runner, with a short-name temporary folder and the project on another drive. Red runs showed which tests failed for the intended reasons, and showed that under a short-name root two alias tests passed only because a different operand was rejected first. A new test pinned a refusal that no test had referenced before. A deliberate mutant, the refusal disabled for one run, proved the new test fails without it. The timing test became a count assertion with its own mutant. The final local full check ran 14,198 tests, 13,255 unit and 943 end-to-end, with 0 failures and the same 19 skips as the previous accepted run, and a manual CI run on the fixed commit passed both jobs on 20 October.
A green local suite was evidence for one filesystem layout. Several rules of the process exist to keep that kind of distinction explicit.
Two loops
Figure 1. The edit loop and the release gate, with each step marked as run in CI, run by a local Gradle task, or not run by the build.
The maintained procedure, work-cycle-docs/work-test-cycle.md, separates "an inner development loop and a Release QA Gate". A full release packet "is reserved for candidate acceptance, not repeated after every edit."
The inner loop has seven steps.
Branch, version and working-tree state are confirmed.
The objective, preserved invariants, affected boundaries, acceptance checks and stop conditions are stated briefly.
Source and callers are inspected, and the failure is reproduced through the real affected boundary where possible.
A coherent correction and focused regression coverage are written.
Focused checks and git diff --check run. The intended cause of each failed assertion is checked before its expectation is changed.
Adjacent integration and relevant deterministic end-to-end checks run before scope widens, especially for authority, persistence and shared policy.
Required local gates and independent review proportional to risk complete before the batch is accepted.
The release gate starts only when a candidate is authorized. It requires a full automated gate on the exact candidate commit, staged artifacts with checksums, an SBOM and attestations, a smoke test of the product installed from the candidate artifact, manual evidence from a real terminal session, and a live audit on two models when model behavior is part of the release claim. The release runbook stages the artifacts first and runs the product checks on what was staged. Failed staging evidence is not repaired in place. The product or process is fixed, the fix is committed, and staging runs again from the new commit.
What one check holds
Full Gradle check is required before a batch that touches runtime behavior, release wiring, public documentation contracts or shared policy is accepted. It holds six gates.
Unit tests, the src/test source set.
Deterministic end-to-end tests, a separate src/e2eTest source set of scripted scenarios with no live model.
Coverage floors through JaCoCo. 82 percent of instructions and 62 percent of branches globally, with package floors of 87 and 67 percent for runtime policy, 80 and 62 percent for safety, and 37 and 39 percent for the secret package, a floor that, by the build file's comment, pins the low coverage measured in June 2026 in place.
A canary scan over test reports and results, which fails if raw privacy canaries leak into generated artifacts.
A release ledger check, which requires the top released CHANGELOG version to equal the build version.
An architecture ratchet of six package-direction rules, with a baseline file of accepted violations that is currently empty.
Up to the commit described here, the passing full checks recorded in October executed between 11,578 and 13,498 unit tests and between 932 and 943 end-to-end tests, and took from about 1 hour 5 minutes to 2 hours 38 minutes on one local machine. The longest run was slowed by another process.
Distinctions kept apart
The procedure and the local working guidance name several things that look alike and are kept apart.
A focused pass is not acceptance. On 9 October a new final-status contract passed its focused and adjacent tests. The required full check then failed 4 of 12,500 unit cases. A cause check found three stale exact-output expectations and one structural assertion pointing at an old location, all consistent with the accepted contract, so those expectations were updated. The rerun completed 12,501 unit cases with no failures and the nineteen existing skips, then failed three end-to-end checks, because a qualification reader rejected the new status event. That run was recorded as "an incomplete failed check, not full acceptance." Only the reader and its fixture were fixed, a regression class covering sixteen malformed or misplaced status events was added, and a fresh full check passed.
An exit code is not a result. The build has reporting lanes, candidateTest and candidateE2eTest, that run with ignoreFailures = true so results are preserved when tests fail. Those lanes can finish with exit code zero while failures remain, and the procedure states that "reporting-oriented candidate test tasks can finish with exit code zero while test failures remain." A separate task, qualityReportGate, turns their summaries into a hard gate. It requires zero failures and errors, instruction coverage of at least 82 percent, zero skipped end-to-end tests, every JSON scenario passed, a Qodana result bound to the current source with no critical issue, and an existing jar.
A passing subset is not a release verdict. A completed offline batch is kept distinct from installed-product, live-model and exact-candidate acceptance. For document-comparison lanes, the live audit runbook adds that "A passing subset is not evidence that either profile or the candidate has passed the full audit."
Review agreement is not execution evidence. In the local working guidance, a review, including one by an automated agent, does not count as execution evidence. In the CI repair and the drive-letter batch of 20 October, code changed after a review finding was run again before the final full check.
Execution success is not answer correctness. The current local guidance adds that runtime execution and verification facts do not show that every requested result was answered correctly.
Red first, then a mutant
A green test proves little until it has been seen to fail for the right reason. Since mid-October several batch records follow one shape. A red run comes before the fix, with the failures checked against their intended causes, then the fix, then a deliberate mutant that disables the new behavior and must turn the test red again. No mutation-testing plugin is involved. The mutants are edits applied to the source for a single run, and the source is restored and checked by hash afterwards.
Review can also catch the fix, and an invalid run is not counted. On 20 October a batch fixed Windows paths that lost their drive letter in the request contract, so a target named with a drive could point at the wrong place. A temporary characterization test recorded the behavior first and was then removed, with its output kept. The plan allowed a second step that mapped absolute targets inside the workspace to relative ones. Review rejected it, because it broke the preparation of forbidden targets, and it was removed before acceptance. One red run was marked invalid because the restored file did not compile, and it was not counted as evidence. The full check passed 14,225 tests, 13,282 unit and 943 end-to-end, and the Windows CI run on the commit took 111.4 minutes, beyond the earlier 90-minute limit.
One record per batch
Each coherent outcome gets one short record with five fields, which are the objective, the invariants and boundaries, the evidence, what was assumed or not tested, and the next action. A condensed version of the October CI repair, reconstructed from its plan and analysis files, shows the shape.
Evidence identity is concrete. A run record holds the full command and arguments, the Java home, the commit and a SHA-256 for every source file. A result record is parsed from the JUnit XML rather than from console output and carries a hash of the log. Runs go to fresh labelled output directories with an isolated home directory per test task, and the run scripts refuse an existing directory, so an earlier result is not overwritten. Failed runs and closed reports are preserved, and current status is updated separately.
By 27 October 2026 the release preparation folder held about 300 dated folders from 5 September onward, a few of them for work after the commit described here. Not every folder is an accepted batch. Some are reviews, designs, investigations or failed attempts kept on purpose.
What is automated, and what is not
The procedure is more complete than its automation.
CI runs on pull requests into, and pushes to, the main and beta branches, or by hand for any pushed branch. On Windows it runs the site tests, unit tests, end-to-end tests, coverage and canary checks and a final check. On Linux it runs only the command and path-identity tests.
Release staging is dispatched by hand with a target commit and version. It refuses a commit that does not match, a dirty tree or a missing CHANGELOG heading, runs clean check and the quality summaries on Windows, builds the artifacts, writes a manifest marked qa-staging-not-a-release and attests the files and the SBOM. The Linux staging job builds artifacts and runs no check.
No workflow at this commit creates a tag or a release, and none has write access to repository contents. CiWorkflowContractTest fails if either staging workflow gains a known release-publishing action or that write access.
qualityReportGate runs in the local maintainer packet, not in CI. The installed-product smoke test, the terminal evidence, the two-model live audit and the checksum and attestation checks after download are manual.
Where the cycle fell short
The opening example contains a lapse. CI ran only on pushes to the main and beta branches and on pull requests into them, and the work stayed on a feature branch with no such run. No CI run was made between 9 July and October, so 132 unit-test failures accumulated without a CI run, and the end-to-end suite had not run on a runner since July. Manual dispatch for any pushed branch was added on 18 October. On 20 October the Windows job's timeout was raised from 90 to 180 minutes, with a contract test that fails on the old value. The release staging job still has a 90-minute limit, recorded as open.
Other limits follow from the repository and the records. Linux coverage in CI is a subset. The batch-record format is a practice, and no tool enforces it. About one folder in sixteen has no analysis file, though most of those hold a plan, a closeout or raw outputs instead. Keeping every run also has a cost. By late October the folder held about 5.7 million files and 104 GB. The current candidate path, including qualityReportGate, which was added on 5 July, has not been run end to end. The last documented release QA packet is the local 0.10.8 packet of 3 July, made under the earlier process. Release readiness is recorded as unestablished.
What transfers
The cycle is specific to one Java codebase. The following parts do not depend on it.
Separate the edit loop from the release gate, and write down which checks belong to which.
Put the required batch gates in one task, and require it before a batch touching shared behavior is accepted.
Check why an assertion failed before changing what it expects.
Watch a new test fail for the intended reason, then disable the behavior for one run and watch it fail again.
Read results from the test reports, not from the exit code of a task built to keep going.
Report fixture, installed and live evidence separately, and never call a subset a verdict.
Record the exact commit and file hashes of every run, keep failed runs, and update status somewhere else.
Run CI where the work actually happens.
Described as of the local development commit de779a78, 27 October 2026, which has not been pushed. Dated examples come from unpublished local batch records of October 2026.

posts.title: Fail Fast, Learn Faster. Instinct, on Purpose
posts.excerpt: This guide shows how to run safe-to-fail experiments in life plus at work. Build a personal system where every attempt either moves you forward or pays you back in information.
headings: What "Fail Fast" Looks Like in Real Life
Turn Instinct Into a Routine. Safe to Fail, Not Foolish
Rails That Keep "Fast" From Sliding Into "Sloppy"
A Five Step Routine to Harness Instinct
Culture That Keeps the Loop Alive
posts.text:
Let's talk about an awkward but powerful concept.
This guide shows how to run safe-to-fail experiments in life plus at work.
People advance by trying, by messing up, and by fixing the mess. Failure appears only after you act. If you stay still, nothing arrives at all. From day one we learn by colliding with the world. Touch a hot pan once and the burn teaches the rule. That burn is instinct. If you block every failure, you gag the oldest teacher alive. Do not silence the instinct, steer it. Build a personal system that does not collapse because it is aligned with reality, where every attempt either moves you forward or pays you back in information, then use that information immediately.
What "Fail Fast" Looks Like in Real Life
Humans and animals develop habits the same way. When an action ends well we tend to keep it, and when it ends badly we tend to drop it. Thorndike called this the Law of Effect, a foundation beneath everyday skill.
Brain also learns through prediction errors. When the world refuses to match your guess, neural machinery issues a simple order, revise the model. Small errors feed rapid updating, and the cerebellum plays a central role in those error signals, which is why a minor stumble can teach faster than a lecture.
Communities that hide or punish errors starve this wiring. Research on Error Management Training shows the opposite works better. Expect slips, invite exploration, and train recovery. Learners taught this way transfer the lesson to new situations more effectively than those trained to avoid every slip.
Turn Instinct Into a Routine. Safe to Fail, Not Foolish
In knotty situations, whether that is a new habit, a creative craft, or yes, a complex initiative at work, you cannot think your way to perfect foresight. You probe reality with small, safe experiments, many tiny bets, each able to break only a small (toy) part of the system, each with a clear rule for what you will do next. The Cynefin framework calls this discovery by safe to fail probes. Nudge the system, observe what survives, follow the survivor.
Rails That Keep "Fast" From Sliding Into "Sloppy"
Fence off danger. Set clear limits on time and scope, for example five people, ten percent exposure, or a sandbox that resets itself.
Build for learning. Write down what a win, a loss, and a no signal outcome would look like before you begin, then decide the next step for each case. Amy Edmondson's work on intelligent failure points to small bets in new territory with learning designed in.
Keep it safe to tell the truth. People need room to ask, to admit, and to try without dread. Psychological safety sits at the core of effective groups, and it lets the instinct to experiment do its job.
Go blameless. After something breaks, write a postmortem that lists contributing factors and fixes the system rather than the person. Openness increases reliability because people share what really happened.
Measure what matters when you are at work. Watch the four DORA outcomes, how long changes take to reach users, how often you deploy, how often changes fail, and how quickly you restore service. Ignore numbers that only look good on a slide.
A Five Step Routine to Harness Instinct
Say what you do not know. Turn a gut feeling into a testable sentence. "If we remove Step 3, at least eighty percent of new users will finish onboarding." If a claim cannot be proven wrong, it cannot teach.
Pick the tiniest test. Use a minimum viable prototype, a brief live trial, a paper sketch, anything that gives a real signal quickly while exposing almost nothing.
Nail the learning rule. Choose one success metric and one guardrail metric, for example completion rate and support requests, then write in advance what results will mean go, tweak, or stop.
Run short loops. Curiosity fades fast, so act while energy is high. Many small, cheap tests beat one large, slow plan.
Look back and lock the choice. Capture one page of learning. Note what surprised you, which assumption died, and what you will do next. Store the note where you can find it so you do not re-argue the same decision later. This record is part of learning faster.
Culture That Keeps the Loop Alive
People need psychological safety, the freedom to try something that might fail without mockery or penalty. That freedom is the backbone of groups that perform well, in families, in communities, and in workplaces. Blameless learning keeps experiments honest. State what broke and why, skip who to blame, publish causes and fixes, and you build strength over time.
Weekly Cadence That Sticks
Monday. Pick one belief to test. Write a single page with the guess, the test, the two metrics, the decision rule, and the owner.
Wednesday. Run the test on a tiny slice of reality, and write down ethical and brand limits so the probe is truly safe to fail.
Friday. Hold a twenty minute review. Decide whether to scale, tweak, or stop, then log the choice and, if you are applying this at work, tie follow ups to the four DORA numbers.
Bottom Line
Trial and error is not a defect to hide, it is the built in learning motor. Aim it with guardrails, shorten each lap, and review on schedule. You will not fail more often. You will learn on purpose, spend little, and gain clear facts. That is how instinct becomes an edge.

posts.title: From a RAG CLI to an Execution Harness
posts.excerpt: How a local retrieval tool called LOQ-J became Talos. The decisions that shaped it, what most of them cost, and what was built and then taken out on purpose.
headings: Decision one. Tools first, checks second
Decision two. An engine that can require a tool call
Decision three. No generic shell tool
Decision six. A living wiki, for 22 days
Decision seven. Clean the tree and publish
Decision eight. A catalog with evidence per profile
posts.text:
In short. Talos began in September 2025 as LOQ-J, a local command-line tool for retrieval over documents. Over thirteen months it became what its README calls "a broader local workspace assistant and execution harness", with a runtime that decides what a model may do. The history is a sequence of decisions, several of them reversals, and the removals say as much as the additions.
Figure 1. LOQ-J, the months with no recorded commits, and the Talos decisions from April to October 2026.
The starting point
The first commit, on 9 September 2025, reads "initial import of LOQ-J v0.1.0". LOQ-J stood for Local-Only Java. It arrived as 57 files, with a picocli command line, Lucene 10 with BM25 and vector search over local documents, a SQLite cache, Ollama for chat and embeddings with qwen3:8b and bge-m3 as defaults, a JavaFX first-run wizard that installed Ollama through winget, and a jpackage target for a Windows installer.
Its default configuration also carried a command allowlist of twenty programs, from git and gradle to powershell, cmd and bash, with a blocklist beside it. No Java code read either list, and both were gone from the default configuration within three days.
The first month added BM25F field boosts, gating for the REPL's own commands, a redactor, a sandbox, a reworked network policy and a service interface for several engines, of which only Ollama worked. The last commit of that period is dated 9 October 2025. The next commit came 172 days later.
Decision one. Tools first, checks second
Work resumed on 30 March 2026 with a modernization plan that reserved a seam for tools. On 31 March, 37 commits added 37 architecture files, two overlapping sets with 22 distinct file names. Among their decisions were command line first, multi-agent orchestration not the primary driver, and approval as a core runtime concept, "not optional glue added later."
On 6 April the project was renamed Talos, a day after a short-lived rename to Loqs. The same day the model first called tools, read_file, grep and retrieve, then write_file and edit_file, with an approval gate for writes. The rename commit records 802 passing tests.
Cost. For nearly three weeks Talos could write files after approval but without a verifier or a task contract. What followed. Between 25 and 29 April came a static task verifier, a task contract, a local turn trace, declarative allow, ask and deny permissions, and a checkpoint before every approved change. Versions 0.9.1 to 0.9.8 cover those five days.
Decision two. An engine that can require a tool call
On 3 May a managed llama.cpp backend arrived, after a design written the same day moved the default away from Ollama. The design gives the reason. It found that Ollama's documented native chat shape "does not expose a required tool-choice control", and a turn that must act needs to require a tool call. It also sets a limit that held from then on. Switching engines "is still not a substitute for Talos runtime control."
Cost. Two backends were maintained side by side for five months, and request controls such as required tool choice and sampling settings were built around the llama.cpp path. What followed. Ollama left the default path with 0.10.6 on 25 June. On 18 October the development branch removed it entirely, deleting 4,401 lines. That last step is recorded only as an owner's rule. A llama.cpp engine had been a stub in September 2025 and was deleted as dead code in April 2026 before it returned as the real backend.
Decision three. No generic shell tool
On 5 May the command execution design stated its first rule, "Do not add a generic shell tool.", and cited OWASP's entry on excessive agency. Typed command profiles and a Gradle command tool followed. On 12 June workspace-declared profiles gained a trust store keyed by a content hash.
Cost. The built-in command set is five Gradle tasks, and anything else needs a declared, pinned profile. What followed. Commands became narrow and named, while the programs they launch still run with the user's permissions. A profile is not a sandbox, and the approval request for a command states that the host network is not isolated.
Decision four. Stop decomposing
Version 0.10.0 was declared a beta candidate on 7 June, with ArchUnit architecture guards. Five candidates followed in three days, the last four with machine-checkable gate ledgers. A full-screen terminal interface was considered and rejected in favor of inline JLine.
A structural decomposition of the turn executor and the tool loop ended on 17 June by an explicit decision, recorded as "diminishing returns" and "the risk of over-fragmenting". Cost. The turn executor was about 2,735 lines at the stop. It has grown to 3,444 since and is the second largest main class at the pin.
Decision five. Narrow the claims
The trust track began on 16 June with an internal audit of the project's own trust claims, which found many of them broader than the code. The first fix was an honesty pass on the documentation, which made the docs state current limits instead of intended ones, under the line "A documented limitation is not an overclaim." Code fixes followed. A full end-to-end audit on 24 June found that no hard-fail gate fired. It also opened seven follow-up findings. One of them, rated high, covered fabricated read and command claims that sit outside the mutation guard.
What followed. A guard for the fabricated git-status case landed within a day, and later work broadened it to other recognized command-output shapes. The README still states that the deterministic correction is strongest for file-mutation turns, and that arbitrary command claims and broad read claims are not completely covered.
Decision six. A living wiki, for 22 days
On 13 June a living wiki was added, with committed pages with evidence frontmatter, a structural lint that ran with the unit tests, a liveness lint against a generated architecture report, and a close gate run by the candidate cut script. It was archived on 5 July. The archiving commit reads "clean up docs before release", and the work-cycle README it added says wiki state is "not part of the public repository contract".
Decision seven. Clean the tree and publish
On 5 July a single commit changed 1,115 files and removed 168,074 lines from the tracked tree. Tickets, reports, research notes, the wiki and 25 numbered architecture documents moved to a local archive, a 1,207-line guidance file left the tracked tree, and four short architecture documents replaced the set. A hygiene test now fails the build if the work-cycle runbooks cite archived tickets or the old wiki gate.
The v0.10.8 tag followed on 6 July, and the README in the tagged tree still called the Windows public beta signed-only. Hours later a commit on the development branch rewrote the install guidance. According to the README at the pin, the 0.10.8 developer beta is published as GitHub Release assets for Windows x64 and Ubuntu or WSL x64, and the Windows assets are unsigned and need an explicit flag to install. A signed release and a winget package are not live.
Cost. The removed history is still in git and in a local archive, but no longer in the tree a reader browses. What followed. The documents that remain are short, and tests pin their load-bearing claims.
Decision eight. A catalog with evidence per profile
Since May a two-model rule has governed live audits, and the release-candidate runbook still requires it when a release claim depends on model behavior. In June three experimental profiles for two more models were added beside the two accepted ones. From 10 to 15 July a deterministic qualification protocol took twelve open-weight models through preflight, admission or full 72-trial campaigns. Six completed a full campaign, and five new experimental profiles joined the catalog.
Cost. The two accepted profiles still rest on an earlier evidence record. GPT-OSS 20B, one of them, scored in the experimental tier on its own 72-trial run in July and keeps its accepted label on that earlier record. The raw qualification packets stay local. What followed. Every selectable profile in the catalog must name its evidence, either a qualification packet or an earlier record, and the catalog refuses to load one that does not.

What converged
From the first Talos design onward, the recorded decisions put authority in the runtime rather than in the model. The three largest later model decisions, the llama.cpp backend, the required tool choice and the qualification protocol, made the model easier to check rather than easier to trust.
There was no generic shell tool. A command allowlist sat in the very first configuration file and never reached code, and when command execution arrived, its design's first rule was the sentence "Do not add a generic shell tool".
The documents shrank in July while the code kept growing, and the claims in them got narrower. No release has followed 0.10.8. The October records end with lines such as "Release readiness remains unestablished."
